title: Lack of exposure to natural light in the workspace is associated with physiological, sleep and depressive symptoms
research_question: To evaluate the effects of exposure or lack of exposure to natural light in a rest/activity rhythm on cortisol and melatonin levels, as well as on psychological variables in humans under natural conditions.

participants.description: 20 female employees (mean age 41.3 ± 11.5 years for 'with window' group, 44.60 ± 22.0 years for 'without window' group) from Hospital de Clínicas de Porto Alegre, southern Brazil. All worked diurnal shifts (8:00 am - 6:00 pm) for at least one year. Excluded males, workers with history of stroke, psychiatric comorbidities, uncontrolled systemic diseases, movement disorders, emergency surgery, illicit drug use, or specific medication use.
participants.recruitment: Employees of Hospital de Clínicas de Porto Alegre

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Two types of workspaces: 'with window' group (10 employees) worked in environments with natural light through a window in addition to electrical lighting; 'without window' group (10 employees) worked in environments with only electrical lighting with no visual contact to the outdoors or outdoor light.

mechanisms: Increased levels of cortisol and lower levels of melatonin are related to several diseases.
Plasma melatonin peaks (acrophase) occur 4-6 hours before the acrophase of the cortisol rhythm, driven by the suprachiasmatic nucleus which is sensitive to light exposure.
Melatonin reduces NF-kB activation and immune-competent cell count, while immune system activation interrupts melatonin production.
Corticosterone increases melatonin synthesis induced by β-adrenoreceptors, suggesting a complex pathway involving the immune system for cortisol and melatonin's influence on mood.
Depression may involve hormonal changes preceding clinical features.
implementation_implications: Recommending exposure to natural light for workers is reasonable to increase benefits for labor and workers.

limitations: Cross-sectional study design limits causal inference.
All participants were women, limiting generalizability to men.
The study was conducted in a specific geographical location (southern Brazil), and findings may be influenced by local factors like season and latitude.
